title: Classroom Roulette: Slides or Students?
author: The Disruptive Educator
summary: Building on Leah Myers's observation that 'if explicit instruction is death by PowerPoint, then teacher autonomy is death by inequity,' this article by The Disruptive Educator argues that debates about slides and teacher autonomy frequently avoid the real issue: excessive instructional variance creates profoundly unequal student experiences within the same school. Low-variance curriculum resources do not eliminate teacher personality or professional judgment; they reduce the harmful inconsistency in content sequencing and resource quality that makes educational opportunity depend on which classroom a student happens to be assigned to. Teachers who share high-quality sequenced materials are freed to exercise professional expertise where it matters most: in the actual enactment of instruction with real students. The piece reframes the aesthetics debate as an equity debate about the 'lesson lottery.'
points: Arguments about instructional aesthetics (PowerPoint, slides, scripts) often mask avoidance of the harder equity question about how much instructional variance is tolerable.
When every teacher builds curriculum from scratch, quality varies because of structural overload, not differing care or expertise.
Research shows high-quality shared curriculum materials can boost student learning by one to two months per year.
Low-variance instruction and teacher personality are not mutually exclusive: teachers still exercise judgment in pacing, explanation, and response to misconceptions.
The 'lesson lottery' means students in different classrooms within the same school encounter fundamentally different instructional quality, compounding unequal outcomes over years.
quotes: If explicit instruction is death by PowerPoint, then teacher autonomy is death by inequity.
Students should not experience fundamentally different chances of success simply because they were allocated to different classrooms.
High-quality curriculum resources do not remove the need for teacher expertise. If anything, they create greater capacity for teachers to exercise that expertise where it matters most.
Autonomy is not virtuous if the outcome is inequitable access to effective instruction.
When every teacher independently builds curriculum from scratch, instructional quality varies not because of differing care or expertise but because of structural overload
